threads.norm: Share your own numbers. Don't tell anyone else what to charge.

pinned.question: What do you get paid per game — and what's actually included?
pinned.body:
Rates for this work are all over the map and nobody can find out what anything is worth without asking a stranger. So: what's your number, what's the format, how long is the game, and does the venue cover your tab?

We'll go first. These are Fat City's real numbers — Canadian dollars, weekday show, roughly three hours on site.

A one-off weekday show is $450. Almost nobody pays that, and it isn't a bluff price — a single night is genuinely the most expensive way to buy this. Nothing amortises. We price it to reflect that.

Booked as a recurring night it's $225. Three or four dates is the minimum that makes sense; twelve booked at once is what we're actually aiming for. There's one step past that: $200 flat if the venue puts a $25 tab behind the bar for the host. We'd rather give the tab than the $25, and further down this thread we'll explain why that trade is better for the venue than it looks.

Weekends, holidays and special events are full rate or higher. A two-host Christmas party starts at $900.

The part that catches new hosts out is the cost side. Budget about $50 a night for licensing games, printing cards and consumables. So on a $225 night you keep $175 for about three hours. On the $200-plus-tab deal you keep $150 and drink for free. Work out your costs before you agree to a number, not after.

That's ours. What's yours?

harvest.prompt: Optional, one tap: add your number to the index.
harvest.index_blurb: What hosts report being paid, as reported. Median and range only, never a recommendation.

unlocks: Why we'd rather give a $25 bar tab than $25 off. A tab costs the venue roughly a third of its face value in actual product — they hand over $25 of perceived value for well under ten dollars of cost. The host counts it as $25. Both sides come out ahead of a straight discount, and it's the easiest concession a manager can say yes to without asking anyone.

Why we push for twelve dates instead of three. A new trivia night takes about six weeks to build a room — the first few are quiet no matter how good the show is. A three-date trial ends right as it starts working, and the venue concludes it didn't. Twelve is the smallest booking that gives the night a fair test. That argument closes more bookings for us than the price does.

The $50 a night nobody quotes for. Game licensing, printing cards and answer sheets, batteries, replacement markers, the odd prize. It's small enough to ignore and it's the difference between a $225 night being worth doing and being break-even once you've driven there. Price your costs in before you name a number, because you won't get to add them afterwards.

Why our one-off price is nearly double the recurring one, and why we don't move on it. A single date carries all the setup, all the travel, all the prep, and none of it amortises across a run. Discounting a one-off to win it means the busiest, most awkward show you'll do all month is also the worst paid. Quote it high and mean it.

pinned.question: How do you walk into a bar that doesn't have trivia yet?
pinned.body:
Everybody's process is different and most of us worked ours out alone. What do you actually say, who do you say it to, and how many times do you go back before you write the place off?

Our angle on this is sideways. Before this was a trivia company it was fifteen years of managing bars and restaurants — which means we've been the manager getting pitched far more often than the host doing the pitching. So we'll go first with what that side of the bar is actually thinking.

Start with when. Walking in at 7pm on a Friday to pitch anything marks you as someone who has never worked in a restaurant. Nobody is going to remember your name, let alone your idea. Tuesday to Thursday, two to four in the afternoon, is the window: lunch is done, dinner prep is under way, and the person you want is on the floor and not yet underwater.

Then who. The bartender is not the decision maker but is absolutely the gatekeeper, and they will be asked afterwards what they thought of you. Be decent to them whether or not they can say yes. The person you want is the GM or the owner, and the useful question is not 'are you the manager' but 'who books your entertainment' — it gets you a name instead of a no.

What a manager is actually worried about, in roughly this order: that you won't show up; that you'll be loud enough to drive off the regulars who are already spending; that the staff will have to work harder for the same money; and only then, somewhere near the bottom, what it costs. Almost every pitch leads with price and format, which answers the least important question in the list. Lead with reliability and with what the night does to a slow room, and you're already ahead of everyone else who came in that month.

The quiet write-off is real, and it usually isn't about the pitch. It's turning up during a rush and not reading the room. It's talking to someone in the weeds. It's a follow-up the same night. Managers rarely say no outright — they say 'send me something' and then don't reply, and most hosts read that as a maybe. It isn't. It's a no that's being polite. The recoverable version is to go back once, in person, a couple of weeks later, having eaten there in between.

[OWNER: replace or extend the above with your own specifics before launching this thread. It is structurally right but it is generic — it reads like advice, not like someone who has stood on that side of the bar for fifteen years. What it needs is yours: the actual pitch that got you a yes, the one that embarrassed you, the thing a rep did that made you write them off on the spot, what your own GM told you about entertainment budgets. One real story is worth the whole section above. This is the single strongest asset Fat City has in this room and nobody else in the space can write it.]
